18. **The balance pass.** With the main systems built, tune them together, starting from the first guesses each item's report lists: the pace of war (sieges, marching, slow absorption, campaign seasons if needed), travel times and the odds of interception and discovery, characters' costs (escorts, storage, ongoing costs), lending, the gift threshold for routine audiences, scoring weights and normalization, starting positions, and game length with the random ending (the default cap and median, weighing what longer games cost in usage against how exciting they stay, "Random ending" under Victory; "Open questions"; "Normalization waits for data" under Scoring). Script games only (seeds 1–100 and 101–200), with the script kings at their strongest. Model games, for what scripts cannot show, such as whether characters' greed and kings' trust settle where the game stays interesting, come afterwards, when Haakon asks. Before tuning, take the power names out of the script kings' rules ("Different data, same rules"): thinking maritime comes from the map (an island, a coastal capital, the fleets it holds); the small powers' fleet levies, peace bonus and tribute, and a proud king denying Great King to small powers, come from rank in the starting data; Babylonia's named rule against Assyria is already replaced in item 8 ("Recognition is earned"), whose thresholds are tuned here. Temperament becomes a setting: the historical archetypes by default, or temperaments rolled per game, in which case kings judge rivals' temperaments from what they do instead of knowing their archetypes. Whether capitals fall in "most" games (item 5 found about half, under the old ending) is judged only after game length is set. Two things to watch while tuning: standing orders, which answer a blow in the season it falls, favour defence on top of walls and sieges, so check that wars still end, and that they still begin, since lost harvests and a lost generation make war dear (item 10+); and commanders are worth what stale orders cost, so check that order travel times make a commander worth his fee and his risk on a distant front, while a small realm may rightly need fewer. Script kings' gifts, bribes and tribute become investments judged by their expected return over a horizon, as in "Gold is a lifeline", replacing the spare-gold and generosity thresholds. Check too that bold and careful characters reach the top of the characters' ranking at comparable rates, and tune until both roads pay ("Bold or careful, one goal" in the Ideas tab). Tune the wealth of a realm: how much the land weighs against gold and goods, comparing win rates per power, whether kings build, give and campaign or sit on their treasure, whether Egypt's mines carry it further than par allows, and what the last seasons look like, since gold sent abroad costs score and darkening omens may make kings stingy at the end ("The wealth of a realm" under Victory; "Scores" under "Economy and resources" in the Ideas tab). In the seasons when the omens are darkest, look by name for four grabs the score pays for in the moment and only hunger or reputation answers: raising taxes, keeping grain from hungry towns, seizing characters' hoards in one's own temples, and leaving fees unpaid; and check that kings still hire envoys and spies then, not only that they stop paying for what will not return. Set the pool's default size from the wake-ups measured since item 8 ("How many characters"). Check too that the courts play distinctly across seeds, with different openings, trade and wars rather than one strategy everywhere ("Each court plays differently" under The world). Watch the markets' purses for both creeping inflation and gold draining away into characters' hoards ("Where gold comes from and where it goes"). Check that no court is starved of servants for want of travellers or of men who speak its language, by how long its letters wait for a carrier, and that fees rise until service pays again when working for oneself pays better ("Where characters are, and what they speak" in the Ideas tab). **Stop for review.**
